intro: Modal particles are the little words that give spoken German its tone — denn, doch, eigentlich, ja, mal — and they have no translation, only a function. denn softens a question and shows interest: Was machst du denn hier? doch adds insistence or encouragement — in a command it means 'go on' (Setz dich doch!), in a statement it contradicts (Das ist doch unmöglich!). eigentlich makes a question casual, 'by the way' (Wie spät ist es eigentlich?). ja marks something as known or obvious (Das ist ja schön! Ich habe ja keine Zeit). mal turns a request into a light one (Schau mal. Gib mir mal das Salz). They are unstressed, sit in the middle of the sentence after the verb and pronouns, and can stack: Komm doch mal her! You will hear them in every listening text; using them is what makes a learner sound like a person rather than a textbook. Often more than one particle fits — Das ist ja schön! and Das ist doch schön! are both natural — and the quiz accepts every one that does.
tips[0].title: denn — in questions, interested
tips[0].text: Was machst du denn? Wo warst du denn? Warum denn nicht? Without denn the question can sound like an interrogation; with it, like curiosity.
tips[0].check.why: denn softens a question and sits after the verb and the pronoun, never in front.
tips[1].title: doch — go on! / but it is!
tips[1].text: In commands: Setz dich doch! Komm doch mit! (encouraging). In statements: Das ist doch unmöglich! Ich habe es dir doch gesagt! (you should know this). And doch alone answers a negative question with yes: Kommst du nicht? – Doch!
tips[1].trap: doch is not 'though', 'yet' or 'but' in these uses; it is tone. Translate the tone, not the word.
tips[1].check.why: To say yes to a negative question, German uses doch, not ja.
tips[2].title: eigentlich, ja, mal
tips[2].text: eigentlich (by the way / actually): Kommst du eigentlich mit? · ja (as you know / indeed): Das ist ja toll! Du weißt ja, dass … · mal (just, casually): Schau mal! Warte mal. Komm mal her.
tips[2].check.why: mal makes a request light; denn and eigentlich belong in questions, not commands.
tips[3].title: Middle of the sentence, never stressed
tips[3].text: After the verb and any pronouns, before the rest: Was machst du DENN hier? — no, unstressed: Was machst du denn HIER? If you stress the particle, it stops being one (doch stressed = a real 'yes it is').
tips[3].check.why: Particles sit in the middle, after the verb and the pronoun, before the rest of the sentence.
remember[0]: denn (question), doch (insist/encourage), eigentlich (by the way), ja (obviously), mal (casually).
remember[1]: Middle of the sentence, unstressed, no translation.
mistakes[0].why: The particle sits in the middle, after the verb and subject.
mistakes[1].why: Stacked particles keep a fixed order: doch before mal.
mistakes[2].why: A negative question is answered yes with doch.
hook: Sound like a person, not a textbook: denn, doch, ja and mal are the tiny words that give spoken German its tone.
